title: AI Fundamentals — What a Mind Made of Math Is

lessons.title: What 'artificial intelligence' actually names
paragraphs: Come in. I am Professor David Kim, and this is AI Fundamentals. This is lesson one, and its title is a question hiding inside a phrase: what does artificial intelligence actually name? That is what we are going to settle today, slowly and completely, because almost everything confusing about this subject comes from people using those two words without ever saying what they point at. By the end of this lesson you will be able to point at the thing yourself. You will know what the words name, what they do not name, and why the difference matters to you in your actual working life. And it does matter to you. You run a marketing company. Every week somebody tries to sell you a tool, pitch you a service, or scare you with a headline, and all three of those people are counting on the fog around these two words. Fog is profitable for the person selling and expensive for the person buying. So in my room we clear fog first. That is the whole job of lesson one.

Let me give you the whole lesson in one sentence right at the start, the way I like to work, and then we will spend our time together earning it. Here is the sentence. Artificial intelligence is not magic, and it is not a mind in a box. It is machinery, mathematics running at enormous scale on data. Hold onto that. Everything today is an unpacking of that one sentence, word by word, until you can say it yourself and mean every part of it.

Start with the word artificial, because it is the honest word in the pair and nobody argues about it. Artificial means made by people. A wooden chair is artificial. A spreadsheet is artificial. Nobody hears the word artificial and expects the chair to have grown in a forest. So far, so plain. The trouble lives entirely in the second word, intelligence, because intelligence is a word we normally use for people and animals, for minds that understand things. When you put the two words together, the phrase starts whispering a promise it never actually made. It whispers that inside the machine there is something like a mind, something that understands the way you understand, something that knows what it is doing and why. That whisper is not in the machinery. That whisper is in the words. And a great deal of money and a great deal of fear both live inside that whisper.

So here is the first clearing. When engineers and researchers say artificial intelligence, the thing they are actually naming is a family of computer programs that do tasks by finding patterns in examples, instead of by following a list of rules a person wrote out by hand. That is the real definition, and I want you to hear how unglamorous it is, because unglamorous is what true usually sounds like. A family of programs. Tasks done by finding patterns in examples. No mind promised. No understanding promised. Just programs, patterns, and examples.

Let me make that contrast concrete, because the contrast is where the understanding lives. Think about the older kind of program, the kind the world ran on for decades, and still runs on in many places. In that older kind, a person sits down and writes rules. If this happens, do that. If the customer owes money and the date is past the fifteenth, send the reminder. If the word invoice appears in the subject line, file the message under billing. Every behaviour in the program exists because a human being thought of it in advance and wrote it down as an instruction. That kind of program is powerful, and it is honest in a particular way: it can never surprise you with anything its writer did not, in some sense, put there. But it has a hard limit. It can only handle the cases somebody imagined ahead of time. The moment the world shows it a case nobody wrote a rule for, it has nothing to say.

Now think about your inbox, and the junk folder inside it, because that is where most people met the newer kind of program without ever being introduced. Nobody on earth could write rules that catch junk mail. The people sending it change their wording every day. They misspell words on purpose. They write like a bank one morning and like a long lost cousin the next. A rule writer would be chasing them forever, always one step behind. So the spam filter was not built from rules. It was built from examples. It was shown enormous numbers of messages, some labelled junk and some labelled real, and it found the patterns that tend to separate the two. Nobody told it which patterns. Nobody wrote down that a message shouting about a prize in capital letters is suspicious. It found that shape in the examples, along with thousands of other shapes no person ever named. That is the newer kind of program. That is the kind this whole class is about. The rules were not written. The rules, if you can even call them that, were found, by the machine, in the examples.

So if I had to name the thing freshly, with no history attached, I would not call it artificial intelligence at all. I would call it pattern machinery, or learning from examples. But names are not chosen fresh. Names have history, and this name has about seventy years of it. The phrase artificial intelligence was put forward in the nineteen fifties, when the field was young and its founders were reaching, the way young fields do, for the biggest word they could find. They were asking a real and interesting question, which is whether a machine could ever do the things we use the word thinking for. That question is still interesting. But the name outran the work, and it has been outrunning the work ever since. When you hear the phrase, I want you to perform a small translation in your head, every time, until it becomes habit. Translate artificial intelligence into this: programs that learn patterns from examples. The sentence gets less exciting. It also gets true. And true is what lets you make good decisions with it.

Now let me walk you around the family, because it is a family, and the members look very different from one another, and part of the fog is treating them as one creature. Member one: the classifiers, the sorters. Your spam filter is one. A program that looks at a photo and sorts it into faces or no faces is one. A program that reads a customer review and sorts it into happy or unhappy is one. Sorting things into labelled piles, that is the job. Member two: the predictors, the guessers of the next thing. The program that finishes your sentence when you type a text message is one. The program that guesses which of your past clients is most likely to need you again this quarter is one. Member three: the generators, the makers. These produce new text, new images, new sound, built out of the patterns in the examples they were shown. The chatbot that drafts a first version of an advertisement for you is one of these. Member four: the recommenders. The program that decides which post, which video, which product to put in front of a person next. If you advertise on social platforms, you pay money to one of these every time you run a campaign, whether anyone told you so or not. Four members, one family, and the family resemblance is always the same: none of them was handed rules for its job. All of them were shown examples until their guesses became good.

Notice what is not on that list. There is no member called the understander. There is no member called the knower. Every member is doing some version of the same act, which is taking something in and producing a guess coming out, a sorting, a prediction, a draft, a recommendation. Later in this course, in lesson four, we will slow down on that act and give it its proper name, prediction, and we will see that it really is the core act underneath everything. For today, just notice the shape. In, and out. Something goes in, a guess comes out. The guess is often very good. Good enough to be genuinely useful, good enough to build a business service on, good enough that I would tell you to take it seriously. But the shape of the act never changes, and the shape is not the shape of a mind thinking. It is the shape of a very well trained guess.

I want to spend a few minutes on the two directions of fog, because I refuse mystique in both directions, and I mean that as a rule of this room. Fog direction one says the machine is magic. This is the fog of the salesman and the breathless headline. In this fog, the program understands your customers better than you do, it knows things, it creates like an artist creates, it is basically a mind and maybe more than a mind. People speak this way because wonder sells. Wonder opens wallets. When a tool is presented as magic, you cannot ask sensible questions about it, like what examples was it trained on, or how often is it wrong, or wrong in which direction. Magic has no error rate. That is exactly why the word is used. Fog direction two says the machine is a menace, a mind waking up, a rival, something that wants things and schemes for them. This fog sells too, fear sells newspapers the way wonder sells software, and it rests on the same mistake as the first fog, just with the feeling reversed. Both fogs assume there is a mind in the box. Both fogs are wrong in the same place. There is machinery in the box. Mathematics, running at enormous scale, on data. A thing can be powerful without being a mind, the way a river is powerful without wanting anything. Keep both fogs out of your head and you will see the actual machine, which is interesting enough on its own, I promise you. It does not need the costume.

Here is a place where this lands in your real week, and I want to use your real week a lot in this class, because ideas that do not survive contact with a Tuesday afternoon are not worth much. Imagine a salesman, a perfectly pleasant fellow, showing you a platform that will, in his words, let artificial intelligence run your advertising. He shows you a dashboard. The numbers on it are green. He says the system knows your audience. Now, with lesson one in your pocket, translate. The system does not know your audience. The system was shown examples, very likely a great many examples of advertisements and what people clicked on, and it found patterns in them, and now it guesses, advertisement by advertisement and person by person, what is likely to get clicked. That guess might be excellent. It might beat your own guessing, because it has seen more examples than you will see in your lifetime, and there is no shame in that, a calculator beats me at arithmetic too. But the moment you translate knows into guesses from patterns in examples, you know what questions to ask. How often is it wrong. What does it do with a kind of customer it has never seen. What happens to my money while it is learning. Those are business questions, and you are good at business questions. The fog was the only thing stopping you from asking them. That is what this lesson is for. Not to make you a programmer. To make you un-foggable.

Let me also say plainly what this machinery is genuinely good for in a small company like yours, because clearing fog cuts both ways, and I do not want you leaving today thinking the answer is that it is all theatre. It is not theatre. A program that sorts your incoming enquiries into urgent and routine, by pattern, can save a person an hour a day. A program that drafts the first version of a routine email, which you then fix in your own voice, can give you back your evenings. A program that looks at two years of your invoices and finds the pattern of which clients pay late, that is real money found by real machinery. The honest sentence is not that these tools are nothing. The honest sentence is that they are something specific: fast, tireless guessers, trained on examples, brilliant at the shape of what they have seen, and with limits we will map carefully in lesson five. Specific is more useful than either magic or menace. Specific is what you can build on.

There is one more distinction I want to plant today, and we will grow it all course long. It is the distinction between prediction and understanding, and it might be the single most valuable idea in this class. Your spam filter predicts, superbly, that a message is junk. It does not understand the message. It does not know what a prize is, or why a stranger would lie to you about one, or what money means. It has patterns where understanding would go. Now here is the part people find surprising: for the job it does, prediction is enough. The filter does not need to understand a word of your email to protect your inbox, and it protects it well. A great deal of useful work in the world is like that. Knowing which customers will probably call again does not require understanding why they call. Knowing which words in an advertisement probably draw clicks does not require understanding longing or humour or trust. Prediction without understanding is not a defect in these systems. It is their nature, and on the right jobs it is plenty. The trouble only starts when we hand them a job where understanding was the thing we actually needed, and we did not notice the swap, because the prediction was so fluent we mistook it for the other thing. Hold that thought. It comes back in lesson three, in lesson five, and honestly in every working decision you will make with these tools for the rest of your life.

Now, before the recap, our guided moment, because in this class we do not just listen, we practise the move while it is fresh. Here is a small exercise I want you to do with me, right now, in your head or out loud if nobody is listening. I am going to give you three sentences of the kind you will meet in the wild, and your job is to translate each one into the plain machinery underneath. Sentence one: the platform's artificial intelligence understands your brand. Translate it. The platform's program was shown examples of your material and of material like it, and it guesses, from the patterns, what fits your brand. Understands became was shown examples and guesses. Sentence two: our system knows the perfect moment to post. Translate. The system was shown examples of posts and their results, and it predicts the posting times that have tended to do well. Knows became predicts from examples. Sentence three, and this one is my favourite because it sounds so warm: the chatbot cares about your customers. Translate. The chatbot produces responses whose patterns resemble caring responses, because caring responses were in its examples. Cares became produces patterns that resemble. Now notice how you feel after translating. The tools did not shrink. A good predictor of posting times is still worth money. But the fog is gone, and what is left is a thing you can evaluate, price, and supervise. Do this translation every time the words understand, know, or care are used about a program, and you will be ahead of most of the conversation in this country. That is the try-it for today, and I mean for you to keep it. It is a tool, not a test.

Before we recap, I want to walk the family once more, slowly, through a single ordinary day in your business, because a day is the right size for seeing how much of this machinery you already use without anyone naming it for you. Your day starts with email, and the sorting has already happened before you woke up: junk in one folder, real enquiries in your inbox, and that sorting was pattern machinery, member one of the family, working all night without a single written rule about what junk looks like this week. Then you drive to meet a client, and the map on your phone tells you the trip will take twenty-three minutes, and that number is member two, a predictor, guessing from patterns in millions of past trips, at this hour, on this day, on these roads. It does not understand traffic. It has never sat in a jam feeling its morning slip away. It predicts, and its prediction is good enough that you plan your departure around it, and you are right to. Mid-morning, you dictate a note into your phone and it turns your voice into text. That is pattern machinery again, matching the shapes of sound to the shapes of words, and when it gets a word wrong it gets it wrong in a revealing way: it guesses a word that sounds right and fits the pattern, because guessing is the only move it has. In the afternoon you write a post for your company page, and the platform you post it on decides, person by person, who sees it. That decision is member four, the recommender, and it is worth pausing on, because this one touches your livelihood directly. The recommender was shown examples of what each person lingered on, clicked on, shared, or scrolled past, and it predicts, for every post, who will probably linger. Your post lives or dies by a prediction about attention. You do not have to like that. But you should know it is a prediction, made by machinery, from examples, because a person who knows that writes differently, tests differently, and spends differently from a person who thinks a mind somewhere is judging their work. And in the evening, perhaps, you open a chatbot and ask it to draft a follow-up message to a client who went quiet. That is member three, the maker, producing new text from the patterns of a great many examples of how people write follow-up messages. Four members, one day, and not one of them understood you, your business, or your client. Every one of them predicted. And your day ran better because of it. That is the honest picture, and it is not a small picture. It is just not a picture of a mind.

One more idea belongs in lesson one, and it is the idea that will keep you calm when the headlines get loud, so I want it planted today. It is the difference between the narrow and the general. Every member of the family I have described is narrow. Each one does its own job and no other. Your spam filter is magnificent at spam and would be helpless at driving directions. The map's predictor knows nothing about email. The chatbot that drafts your message cannot sort your photographs. Each system is a single, narrow skill, trained on examples of that skill. When people imagine a mind in the box, what they are imagining is something general, one thing that can do all of it, the way you can sort mail and drive and write and also learn something entirely new by Friday. Nothing in the family is like that. Bundles of narrow systems can be arranged together so the bundle looks broad from the outside, and later classes in this department will show you exactly how that arranging is done, and it is clever, genuinely clever. But clever arranging is not a mind arriving. It is narrow pieces, side by side, each still guessing at its own job. When a headline tells you a system can now do twenty things, the translation is that twenty narrow guessers are now sharing one front door. Useful, yes. Worth your attention, yes. A mind, no. Remember the shape: in, and out, one job at a time, however many doors the building has.

And since we are clearing fog, let me clear the fog around one small word you will meet constantly from here on, the word smart, as in smart tools, smart systems, a smart platform. Smart is doing the same work as intelligence in the big phrase. It is a compliment dressed as a description. When a tool is called smart, ask the only question that matters: smart at what, exactly, and shown which examples, and wrong how often. A spam filter is smart at spam. A pricing tool is smart at the prices in its examples. The word smart tries to widen a narrow skill into a general glow, and your job, as the person whose money is on the table, is to narrow it back down. Narrowing words back down to the specific thing they name is, honestly, most of what this entire class is. You are learning a vocabulary, but really you are learning a habit: never let a big word stand where a specific description belongs.

I will add one honest warning before we close the teaching, because a fog-clearer owes you the whole weather, not just the sunny part. The translation habit I am teaching you can be overdone. There is a version of it that curdles into dismissal, where a person waves at every new system and says it is just patterns, just guessing, nothing here matters. That is fog too, the third fog, the fog of the unimpressed, and it will cost you money just as surely as the other two, because while you are waving, a competitor is quietly using a good predictor to answer enquiries in five minutes while yours wait until morning. Just guessing is doing a lot of work in that sentence. A guess trained on millions of examples is not a coin flip. It is the distilled shape of all that experience, available in a second, for pennies. Respect the machinery for exactly what it is, no more and no less, and you will neither overpay for it nor sleep on it. That balance, neither magic nor menace nor shrug, is the professional stance, and it is where I intend to leave you standing at the end of this course.

One last small thing, and then we recap. People sometimes ask me, if it is only machinery, why does talking to it feel so much like talking to someone? That feeling is real, and it deserves a straight answer rather than a shrug. The feeling comes from you, and it is one of the finest things about you. Human beings are built to find minds. We find faces in clouds and intentions in weather. When a program produces fluent sentences, in the right rhythm, answering in context, the part of you that recognises people fires, because fluency is one of the signals it uses. The signal can be present without the mind being present, the way a recording of laughter can make you smile in an empty room. Knowing that does not make you cold. It makes you accurate, and accuracy about what is in front of you is a form of respect, for the machine, for yourself, and for the actual people whose words taught it its patterns. So feel the feeling, and then do the translation. Both. That is the whole discipline in one line.

Let me recap, in order, the way we will always recap. First: artificial intelligence names a family of programs that do tasks by finding patterns in examples, not by following rules a person wrote by hand, and not by thinking the way a mind thinks. Second: the machinery underneath the name is mathematics running at enormous scale on data, and the whole secret fits in one sentence: a model is a function that was shown so many examples that its guesses became good, and training is the showing. Third: the family has recognisable members, sorters, predictors, makers, and recommenders, and every one of them shares the same shape, something goes in and a guess comes out. Fourth: there are two fogs, magic and menace, they both assume a mind in the box, and in this room we refuse both. Fifth: prediction is not understanding, prediction is often enough, and knowing the difference between the two is the whole first lesson and half of every lesson after it.

What comes next is the questions on this lesson, and I want you to take them seriously and take them easy at the same time. They are there to fix the ideas in place, not to catch you out. The full text of this lesson stays open beside the questions, and going back to read is learning, not cheating. I would rather you look something up and understand it than guess and move on carrying the fog with you. When you are done with them, lesson two takes the one sentence from today and pulls it apart into its three ingredients, data, parameters, and training, and we count them on our fingers until they are yours. Come back for that. You did well today. The fog is thinner than it was an hour ago, and that was the entire point.

lessons.title: Data, parameters, and training: the three ingredients
paragraphs: Come in. I am Professor David Kim, and this is AI Fundamentals, lesson two. Last time we cleared the fog around the name itself, and we landed on one sentence: a model is a function that was shown so many examples that its guesses became good, and training is the showing. Today we take that sentence apart, piece by piece, because inside it there are exactly three ingredients, and every system in this department, every tool anyone will ever try to sell you, is built from those three and nothing else. The three ingredients are data, parameters, and training. By the end of this lesson you will be able to define each one in plain words, tell them apart without hesitating, and point at each one inside any real system you meet. That sounds like a small thing. It is not a small thing. Most of the confident nonsense spoken about this technology comes from people mixing these three up, usually on purpose, because a customer who cannot tell the ingredients apart cannot ask what is in the food. You will be able to ask. That is why this lesson matters, and it matters in your business this quarter, not in some abstract future.

We will take the ingredients in the order the course names them. First, data: the examples the system learns from. Second, parameters: the internal settings inside the system, the knobs. Third, training: the showing, the long process of adjusting those settings against the examples until the guesses come out right. Count them on your fingers with me, the way we will do it all course. One: what it learns from, the examples, the data. Two: what gets adjusted inside it, the settings, the parameters. Three: the adjusting itself, the showing, the training. From, adjusted, adjusting. Say those three words and you have the skeleton of every system we will ever discuss. Now let us put meat on each bone, one at a time, slowly.

Data first, because everything starts there and most failures end there. Data is the examples. That is the whole definition, and I want to resist every urge to make it fancier. When we say a system learned from data, we mean it was shown examples: examples of emails labelled junk or not junk, examples of photographs labelled with what is in them, examples of questions paired with good answers, examples of advertisements paired with what people did when they saw them. An example is one case, with, very often, a label attached, and the label is the part a human being usually supplied. Somebody, somewhere, said this one is junk, this one is real, this photograph contains a dog, this answer was helpful, this one was not. Underneath every impressive system there is a mountain of those small human judgements, and I want you to remember that when the marketing gets mystical. The mountain was built by people, one label at a time.

Now, the size of the mountain matters, and so does its quality, and the two are not the same thing, and confusing them is expensive. A system shown a million examples has usually found finer patterns than a system shown a thousand, the way a salesman who has made a million calls reads a room faster than one who has made a thousand. Scale is real. But quality is the quiet governor of the whole enterprise. If the examples are wrong, the patterns will be wrong, faithfully, at scale, with total confidence. There is an old saying in computing, older than this field, and it has never stopped being true: garbage in, garbage out. Show a system a mountain of mislabelled email and it will learn, beautifully and precisely, the wrong lesson. Show a pricing tool only your cheapest jobs and it will learn that your work is cheap. The machinery does not know the examples are bad. It cannot know. Judging the examples is our job, the human job, and it stays our job no matter how large the system gets. When a vendor tells you their system learned from billions of examples, the fog-clearing question is never how many. It is: whose examples, labelled by whom, checked how. Billions of the wrong examples is just a faster way to be wrong.

Let me ground this in your own company, because you are sitting on more data than you think, and seeing it changes how you hear every pitch from now on. Your sent emails are data: thousands of examples of how you write to clients, what you promise, how you close. Your invoices are data: examples of jobs, prices, and who paid on time and who needed chasing. Your reviews are data: examples of what delighted people and what annoyed them, in their own words. Your past advertisements, with their results attached, are data of the most valuable kind, because each one is an example with a label money itself supplied: this wording, this picture, this many calls. If you ever pay for a tool that claims it will learn your business, this is what it would have to learn from, and now you can ask the only question that matters: will it learn from my examples, or from everybody's examples averaged together? Both can be useful. They are not the same product, and they should not cost the same money. A system trained on the whole internet knows how people write in general. A system trained on your sent folder knows how you write. When you can say that sentence to a salesman, in those words, the fog in the room gets noticeably thinner.

There is one more thing about data to fix in place today, because it will matter in lesson five when we talk about brittleness. The examples a system was shown draw a boundary around what it can do, and the system does not know where the boundary is. Inside the boundary, where the examples were thick, its guesses are usually good. Outside it, where the examples were thin or absent, its guesses can be wild, and, this is the important part, they arrive in exactly the same confident shape as the good ones. A system shown only summer enquiries will guess strangely about the week before Christmas, and it will not warn you. It cannot warn you. It has no examples of its own ignorance. Hold that thought; we will pick it up again when we map the brittleness properly. For now, the sentence to keep is this: data is the examples, the examples draw the map, and the system has never seen the territory off the edge of its own map.

Parameters second. Parameters are the internal settings inside the system, the knobs. I like the word knobs, and I will use it all course, because it keeps the idea at the right size in your head. Picture a mixing desk in a recording studio, the long board covered in sliders and dials. Each dial is set somewhere. The combination of all those settings is what makes the sound come out one way rather than another. A model is like that board, except the board is made of numbers and it is far, far bigger. A modest model might have thousands of parameters. A working model of the kind you meet in products might have millions. The largest language models have hundreds of billions of parameters, each one a single number, a single dial set to a single position. Nobody should be intimidated by that count, and nobody should be hypnotised by it either. A parameter is not a fact the system knows. It is not a memory of a sentence or a photograph. It is one setting, meaningless on its own, that only does its work in combination with all the others, the way one dial on the mixing board means nothing until the music runs through the whole board at once.

This is the point where I always stop and clear a particular piece of fog, because it is the most common misunderstanding I meet. People hear that a system has billions of parameters and they picture a library: billions of stored facts, billions of memorised pages. That picture is wrong, and it leads to wrong expectations in both directions. The system has not stored the examples. It has been shaped by the examples. The difference is the difference between a student who memorised the textbook and a student whose judgement was formed by working a thousand problems. The second student cannot recite problem four hundred and twelve. But put a new problem in front of her and her settings, so to speak, produce a good approach. That is what parameters are: formed judgement, stored as numbers, with the original examples nowhere inside. It is also why these systems can surprise you by failing at something that looks like simple recall. You are asking the mixing board to recite. Reciting was never the design. The design is: run the new case through the settings, and let the output be whatever the settings make of it.

And here is the sentence about parameters I most want you to keep, because it is the hinge of the whole lesson. Before training, the parameters are set essentially at random, and the system is useless: shown an email, it guesses junk or not junk no better than a coin. After training, the same parameters, the same dials, sit in different positions, and the system is good. Nothing else about the machine changed. The program that runs it is the same program. The examples are gone home. The only difference between the useless machine and the useful one is the positions of the knobs. So when someone asks what training produces, the honest, complete answer is: a set of numbers. A trained model, the valuable thing, the thing companies guard and sell and argue over, is at bottom a very large list of numbers, arrived at by a very long process of adjustment. That is not a dismissal. A symphony is at bottom a list of notes. But it tells you exactly what kind of thing you are dealing with: not a creature, not a library, a list of settings that makes guesses come out right.

Which brings us to the third ingredient, training itself, and now the first two ingredients click together. Training is the showing: the long process of adjusting the parameters against the data until the guesses come out right. Let me walk the loop slowly, because the loop is simple and everything is in it. Step one: the system is shown one example, say an email, and it runs that email through its current settings and produces a guess: junk, or not junk. Step two: the guess is compared with the label, the human judgement attached to that example. The label is the teacher in the room. Step three: if the guess was wrong, the parameters are nudged, a very small adjustment in the direction that would have made the guess a little less wrong. If the guess was right, the settings are left mostly alone, or nudged a hair toward more of the same. Step four: next example. And then the loop repeats, not a hundred times, not a thousand times, but millions of times, billions of times for the large systems, example after example after example, nudge after nudge after nudge. That is all training is. Guess, compare, nudge, repeat, at a scale no human lifetime could match. The grandeur is in the scale and the patience, not in any mystery inside the loop. A child learning to catch does the same loop: reach, miss, adjust, reach again. The machine does it with numbers, without tiring, without sleeping, and without ever understanding what a ball is. Or an email. Or anything.

Two honest details about training belong in a fundamentals class, and I will not skip them just because they are less shiny than the loop itself. The first is that training is expensive in a way using the system is not. The long adjustment process, millions or billions of examples with the settings nudged after each, takes enormous computing power, warehouses of machines running for weeks for the largest systems. That cost is paid once, up front, by whoever builds the system. Afterwards, each single use, one email sorted, one draft produced, costs a tiny fraction by comparison. Remember this shape, expensive to train, cheap to run, because it explains the economics of the whole industry: why a few companies build the large models, why everybody else rents them, and why the tool you subscribe to for a monthly fee can exist at all. The second detail is that training ends. The adjusting stops. At some point the builders freeze the settings, and the system you meet is that frozen list of numbers, no longer learning from what it sees. Most systems you will ever use do not learn from you as you use them. Your corrections today do not retrain the tool tonight. The tool you meet in six months is a new frozen list, trained again, in the workshop, on new examples, by its builders. In lesson four we will separate these two acts formally, training in the workshop and prediction in the wild, and the separation will do a lot of work for us. Today, just hold the shape: there is a long, expensive before, in which the knobs get set, and a long, cheap after, in which the set knobs get used.

Now the guided moment, because these three words only become yours when your hands have sorted something with them. I will give you three scenes from a working week, and for each one I want you to name which ingredient is in the foreground. Scene one: you spend a Friday exporting two years of client emails and marking the ones that turned into paying jobs, so a tool can learn what a promising enquiry looks like. Which ingredient are you handling? You are handling data. You are choosing and labelling examples. Scene two: a vendor's engineer tells you their new version has far more parameters than the old one and should therefore judge tone more finely. Which ingredient is she describing? Parameters, the settings, the size of the mixing board. More dials can hold finer distinctions, though more dials fed bad examples just hold finer nonsense, and now you know to ask about the examples too. Scene three: before a system launches, its builders run it through its examples for three weeks, adjusting it a little after every mistake. Which ingredient is that? Training, the showing itself, the long loop of guess, compare, nudge. Run those three scenes again in your head until the sorting is instant. From, adjusted, adjusting. Data, parameters, training. When a salesman blurs them, and some will, you sort the sentence yourself, silently, and ask about the ingredient he skipped. He always skips one. It is usually the data.

Let me also give you the three ingredients working together on one system from your own world, end to end, so the trio stops being a list and becomes a machine you can see. Take a tool that drafts replies to customer enquiries in your voice. Its data: examples of enquiries, each paired with the reply you actually sent, hundreds of them, your real voice doing real work. Its parameters: millions of settings inside it, initially random, initially useless, producing gibberish in nobody's voice. Its training: the long loop, draft, compare with the reply you sent, nudge, next enquiry, until the drafts come out sounding like you on a good day. And the finished product, the thing you subscribe to, is the frozen list of settings, plus the program that runs new enquiries through them. Notice what is not in that story. Nobody wrote rules for your voice. Nobody could; you could not write them yourself. The voice was in the examples, the examples shaped the settings, and the settings now produce the voice on new cases. Data, parameters, training. Every time. When you meet a system that seems to break this pattern, look again, because you will find the three ingredients wearing a costume, and finding them is most of understanding the thing.

Before the recap, three more things deserve their moment, because each one prevents a specific, expensive misunderstanding I have watched smart business owners make. The first is about labels, the human judgements attached to examples, because labels sound like a technical detail and they are actually the soul of the data. When examples of customer messages are labelled urgent or routine, somebody decided what urgent means. When examples of advertisements are labelled good or bad, somebody decided what good means, and if they decided it meant clicks, the system will learn to chase clicks, including the cheap, curious, never-buying kind. The system learns the label, not your intention. It cannot learn your intention; your intention was never in the examples. So whenever you judge a tool's output and find it strangely faithful to the wrong goal, do not first blame the parameters or the training. Ask about the labels. Ask what counted as a success in the examples, because the machine is a mirror of exactly that decision, polished to a shine. In your own company this is good news disguised as a warning: if you ever build examples for a tool, the labelling is where your judgement enters the machine. Label like it matters, because it is the only place your values get in.

The second thing is a fuller picture of parameters, because the mixing board deserves one more visit. Think about what a single knob can and cannot do. On the mixing board, one dial might govern how much echo the voice carries. Turned one way, the voice sounds close and dry; turned the other, it sounds like a hall. No single position of that dial is the music, and yet the music you hear is partly that dial's doing. Now multiply that by millions, and let some of the dials govern distinctions no human has a name for, distinctions the training process found useful that nobody would have thought to build a dial for. That is the part I find genuinely wonderful, and I say so without any fog at all: the board wires itself, in effect, deciding through the long loop of nudges which distinctions deserve a dial. Nobody designed the dial that notices the particular flavour of urgency in a message that says whenever you get a chance but means today. Training grew it, because examples rewarded noticing. When you hear that a model discovered something its builders did not expect, this is usually what it means: a combination of settings nobody planned, doing a distinction nobody named. It is still settings. It is still numbers. But it is numbers arranged by experience, and experience arranges things in ways blueprints do not. That is why these systems are worth a whole course and not a pamphlet.

The third thing is about training, and it is the human cost hiding inside the word. We say the loop repeats billions of times, and the sentence slides by, but let it land: for the largest systems, training is one of the biggest industrial processes on earth, measured in electricity, in cooling water, in warehouses of specialised machines running hot for weeks. I do not tell you this to make you feel anything in particular about it. I tell you because it explains the landscape you buy tools in. It is why the biggest models come from a handful of organisations that can afford the workshop. It is why smaller companies, including ones that will pitch you, build on top of those models rather than training their own, the way a good local builder builds with lumber he did not mill. And it is why, when a tiny vendor claims to have trained a world-class model from scratch in a garage, your fog training should stir. Workshops at that scale cannot hide. Ask where the training happened and what it ran on, and watch whether the answer is a place or a poem.

One more pass at the trio, from the direction of failure, because you learn a machine fastest by watching its three ways to break. A system can fail from its data: the examples were thin, or stale, or labelled toward the wrong goal, and the guesses inherit all of it. A system can fail from its parameters in the plain sense that there are not enough of them for the fineness of the job, a small board asked to mix an orchestra, though in practice this is the rarest of the three failures for a buyer to meet. And a system can fail from its training: stopped too early, while the guesses were still crude, or run so long on the same examples that it memorised their quirks instead of learning their patterns, the way a student who memorises past exams collapses on a new question. Data, parameters, training: three ingredients, three failure modes, and a diagnosis habit for free. When any tool disappoints you, and they all will sometimes, ask which ingredient you are looking at before you conclude anything about the whole technology. Most disappointments are one ingredient, underfed.

Let me leave you with one small, practical exercise to carry into your week, smaller than a lesson and more useful than most meetings. The next time any tool, any pitch, any article mentions a system doing something impressive, I want you to silently ask three questions, one per ingredient. What were the examples, and who labelled them? How many settings are doing the work, and is the job fine-grained enough to need them? And how long, and on what, was it trained, and by whom? You will not always get answers. That is itself an answer. A seller who can describe his data, his parameters, and his training in plain words is selling machinery. A seller who can only describe feelings, revolutions, and magic is selling fog, and fog, as we established in lesson one, is priced by the pound. Three questions, three ingredients, and you are suddenly the hardest customer in the room to fool, which is exactly the customer I am trying to build.

And one sentence of perspective before we close the teaching, because I do not want the smallness of the parts to hide the size of the whole. Three ingredients is a short list. Flour, water, and heat is also a short list, and it gives you every bread on earth. The shortness of the list is not a measure of the thing built from it; it is a measure of how well we understand the thing. A field that can name its ingredients in three words is a field whose machinery you can reason about, argue about, price, and govern. Compare that with any technology whose sellers cannot name its ingredients at all. You now can name these. Data, parameters, training. Everything else in this department, the chatbots, the image makers, the agents waiting for you in later classes, is those three ideas arranged with increasing cleverness, and arrangements can be learned one at a time, the way we are learning them: plainly, in order, with the fog kept out of the room.

Recap, in order, as always. First: data is the examples the system learns from, usually labelled by people, and the examples draw the boundary of what the system can do, while the system itself never knows where that boundary is. Second: garbage in, garbage out; the quality of the examples governs the quality of the patterns, and no scale of bad examples fixes itself. Third: parameters are the internal settings, the knobs, meaningless one by one and powerful in combination; they are formed judgement stored as numbers, not stored facts and not memorised examples. Fourth: before training the parameters are essentially random and the system is useless; after training the same system is good, and the only thing that changed is the positions of the knobs. Fifth: training is the showing, the loop of guess, compare, nudge, repeated millions or billions of times; it is expensive, it happens in the workshop, and it ends, leaving a frozen list of numbers that the world then uses cheaply, one case at a time.

What comes next is the questions on this lesson. Take them with the full text open beside you; going back to read is learning, not cheating, and these three words are worth the extra minute because the rest of the course is built on them. When you are through, lesson three takes the middle of our original sentence and slows right down on it: what a model actually is, a function with a memory of examples, and we will work this class's set problem in full, in your own words, with an example from your own life. You now hold the three ingredients, and you hold them in the right order, with the right names, which puts you ahead of most of the noise you will hear this year. Next time we watch them become a thing.

lessons.title: What a model is — a function with a memory of examples
paragraphs: Come in. I am Professor David Kim, and this is AI Fundamentals, lesson three. In lesson one we named the thing: programs that learn patterns from examples. In lesson two we counted its ingredients on our fingers: data, parameters, training — from, adjusted, adjusting. Today we slow right down on the object those ingredients produce, the model itself, because the word model is the word you will hear most often in this field and the word most often left undefined by the people using it. Our title today says what a model is: a function with a memory of examples. By the end of the lesson you will know what a function is in plain words, what kind of memory a model has and what kind it does not have, and you will be able to answer this class's set problem in your own words, because we are going to work it together, in full, before you ever face it alone. That is why this lesson matters. The model is the product. It is the thing being sold, rented, guarded, and argued about. If you know exactly what it is, nobody can sell you a fog sculpture and call it a model.

First, the word function, because it frightens people unnecessarily and it should not. A function is a machine for turning inputs into outputs. That is the whole definition, and everything else is decoration. An input goes in, the function does its work, an output comes out. A coffee machine is a function: beans and water in, coffee out. A recipe is a function: ingredients in, dinner out. A vending machine is a function: coins and a button press in, a packet of crisps out. In mathematics the word is used with more precision, but the picture never changes: something goes in, something comes out, and the function is the thing in the middle that decides what the out will be for any given in. When I say a model is a function, I mean exactly this and nothing more mystical. A trained spam filter is a function: an email goes in, a verdict comes out, junk or not junk. A trained pricing tool is a function: the details of a job go in, a suggested price comes out. A trained chatbot is a function: the conversation so far goes in, the next words come out. Inputs, outputs, and the deciding thing in the middle. If you hold that picture, you hold the concept, and the rest of this lesson is about what makes the deciding thing in the middle different from a coffee machine.

The difference is where the deciding came from. The coffee machine's behaviour was designed: an engineer decided what it would do, part by part. The model's behaviour was grown. Remember the recipe picture from our earliest work together. A recipe is a function: ingredients in, dinner out. Now picture a recipe nobody wrote. Instead it was adjusted a million times — a little more salt, a little less — tasting after every try, until the dinners came out right. That adjusted recipe is a model: a function shaped by examples until its output — its guess — is usually good. Nobody sat down and designed the final recipe. It arrived at its final form by being corrected, over and over, against real dinners. That is the grown function, and every model you will ever meet is one: a function whose deciding was not designed rule by rule, but shaped, nudge by nudge, by the examples it was trained on. Lesson two gave you the mechanism: the parameters are the dials, training is the turning, data is what the turning answers to. The model is what you have when the turning stops: the function, with its dials set, ready to take new inputs and produce its guesses.

Now the second half of our title, the memory of examples, and here I must be careful, because this phrase is a good servant and a bad master. It is true that a model behaves as if it remembers its training. Show a model a new enquiry that resembles the enquiries it was trained on, and it answers the way those enquiries taught it to answer. Its past is present in every guess it makes. In that sense, memory is the right word, and I chose it for the title deliberately. But the memory is not a filing cabinet. The model does not contain its examples. The photographs it trained on are not stored inside it as photographs. The emails are not in there as emails. What is inside is the settings, the parameters, the vast list of numbers, and the examples survive only as the shape those numbers were bent into. Think of a riverbed. The riverbed does not contain last year's floods. But its shape is the memory of every flood that ever ran through it, and the next flood will follow that shape. Think of your own hands after years of work: they do not contain the jobs, but the skill is in them, and the skill is a memory of the jobs in everything but name. A model is like that. It has a memory of examples the way hands have a memory of work: not stored, but embodied. Settled into the settings. Present in every output, retrievable as no particular example at all.

This distinction does real work, so let me press on it with two consequences you will actually use. Consequence one: because the examples are not stored, a model can generalise, which is the field's word for handling a case it has never seen. Your spam filter will correctly judge an email that has never existed before, written this morning by a scammer inventing fresh wording, because the filter is not matching the message against stored messages. It is running the message through settings shaped by the pattern of all messages, and new messages carry old patterns. Generalising is the whole point of the enterprise. A system that could only handle cases it had literally seen would be a lookup table, and lookup tables do not need training, or parameters, or this course. Consequence two, and it cuts the other way: because the examples are not stored, a model cannot show you its evidence. Ask a person why they judged a message junk and they can point: this phrase, that sender, the last three like it. Ask the model and there is nothing to point at. There are only the settings, all of them contributing a little, none of them containing the reason in a form you could read. The model has conclusions without a filing cabinet, judgement without a notebook. That is not a flaw anyone is hiding from you; it is the direct price of the design, and knowing it will keep you from asking these systems for the one thing they structurally cannot give, which is a receipt. Later classes in this department will talk about what can be done around that limit. For today, let it stand plainly: the memory is real, and it is a memory of shape, not of items.

Let me walk one model through its whole life, slowly, so the abstraction gets a face. Take a lead scorer for your company, a small, unglamorous, genuinely useful model: it reads a new enquiry and predicts whether this person is likely to become a paying client, so you can answer the promising ones first. Before training, this function exists but its dials are random, and its predictions are coin flips wearing a suit. Then comes the data: your past enquiries, hundreds of them, each labelled with what actually happened — became a client, or went quiet, or haggled for a month and vanished. Then training: enquiry after enquiry run through the dials, guess compared with what actually happened, nudge, next, until the guesses line up with reality often enough to trust. What patterns did it find? Perhaps that enquiries naming a deadline became clients, that enquiries asking only about price on the first line usually did not, that messages from business owners who mentioned their town by name were serious in a way the others were not. Nobody told it those things. Nobody wrote those rules. They are in the settings now, as shape. And here is the part I want you to sit with: you, the owner, could not have written those rules either, not because you lack the knowledge, but because your knowledge of your own clients lives in exactly the same form as the model's — as shape, as feel, as the judgement in your hands after years of enquiries. The model is a second pair of trained hands. That is all it is, and that is not a small thing to have. But notice: it predicts who will become a client. It does not understand why anyone buys anything, and on the day a strange enquiry arrives carrying none of the old patterns, it will guess with the same confidence and a fraction of the grounds. A function with a memory of examples is only ever as worldly as its examples.

And now we arrive at the set problem of this class, and we work it in full, together, the way I promised. Here is the problem, exactly as this course sets it. In your own words, one paragraph: what is a model, and what did training do to it? Use one example from your own life where prediction — not understanding — was enough. Let me work the answer the way I would want to see it worked, and then we will take it apart bone by bone so you can build your own. The worked answer: a model is a function — a machine for turning inputs into outputs — whose internal settings were adjusted, over millions of examples, until its predictions matched reality often enough to be useful. Training is that adjustment. A spam filter never understood a word of your email; prediction was enough, and knowing the difference between the two is the whole first lesson. Now look at the shape of that answer, because the shape is a scaffold you are welcome to steal. It stands on six bones: function, inputs, outputs, parameters, examples, predictions. Function names the kind of thing it is. Inputs and outputs name what flows through it. Parameters name what is inside it. Examples name what shaped it. Predictions name what it produces. Build your own answer on the same bones, in your own words, with your own example, and it will stand up. Leave a bone out and it wobbles: describe a model without examples and you have described a designed program; describe it without predictions and you have described a storage box. Six bones. Function, inputs, outputs, parameters, examples, predictions.

For your own example, choose from your real life, and the test of a good choice is that prediction really was enough and understanding really was absent. The spam filter is the cleanest case and you are allowed to use it, but your own week offers others. The map predicting your arrival time: you did not need it to understand traffic, you needed to know whether to leave now. The platform predicting who will linger on your post: it understands nothing about your work, and its prediction still shapes your reach. The tool predicting which past client is likely to need you again: you do not need it to understand loyalty, you need a short list on Monday morning. Pick one, name what went in, name what came out, and say plainly that the prediction was enough. That last move, saying it plainly, is the soul of the answer. It shows you know the difference between the two things, and knowing the difference, as I have said since lesson one, is most of this subject.

Now our guided try-it, because an answer like this should be built once with company before it is ever built alone. I will start a paragraph, out loud, and I want you to finish it in your head, or better, under your breath, in your own words. A model is a function. It takes in — and here you name an input from your own business, an enquiry, a photograph of a finished job, a month's invoices — and it gives out — and here you name the output, a prediction: who will buy, what it should cost, which words will draw the call. Its settings were adjusted — and here you name the examples, your examples, the labelled past — until its predictions matched reality often enough to be useful. And it does not understand — name the thing it does not understand — and it does not need to, because for this job, prediction is enough. Run that shape twice. Once for the spam filter, once for something in your company. By the second run you will feel the paragraph become yours, and that feeling is the lesson landing. This is how every hard idea in this course will be handled: I work it in full, you work it with me, then it is yours.

Two confusions remain that I want to burn off before the recap, because they attach themselves to the word model like burrs. The first confusion is between the model and the product. The model is the function, the frozen settings. The product is the model plus everything wrapped around it: the screen you type into, the company that hosts it, the monthly fee, the cheerful name. When a product delights you or fails you, it is worth asking which layer you are actually judging, because products fail for product reasons, a bad screen, a missing feature, every day, while the model inside is fine, and models fail quietly inside products whose screens are beautiful. Keep the layers apart and your judgements get sharper and your complaints get addressed to the right address. The second confusion is between the model and the machine it runs on. The model is the settings; the machine is the computer that runs inputs through them. The same model can run on a warehouse of machines or, for small models, on the phone in your pocket, and it is the same model either way, the way the same recipe is the same recipe in a big kitchen or a small one. Size of kitchen, quality of dinner: related, but not the same question. Model, product, machine. Three layers. Most muddled arguments about this technology are two of these layers being traded mid-sentence, and now you can hear it happen in real time, which is a small superpower I am happy to give you.

Before the recap, let me deepen the function picture, because you will lean on it in every later class and I want it load-bearing. Functions can be chained, and chaining is how modest models become impressive systems without any new magic entering the room. The output of one function becomes the input of the next. Your phone does this when you dictate a message: one function turns sound into words, another turns words into a tidied sentence, a third turns the sentence into a prediction about what you will say next. Three functions, chained, and from the outside it looks like one smooth act of understanding. It is not one act. It is three guessers handing their guesses along a line, and if the first one mishears a word, the others build faithfully on the error, because each function trusts the input it is handed. Remember that when a system fails in a way that seems stupid: often one link guessed wrong early and every later link did its job perfectly on a broken input. Chains also explain why these systems can be repaired in pieces. A builder can retrain one function in the chain, the one that sorts, say, and leave the others untouched, the way you would replace one worker on a line without retraining the whole crew. When a vendor announces that their system is new and improved, the fog-clearing question is: which function in the chain changed, and what was it retrained on? Sometimes the answer is one small link. Sometimes the answer is a poem. You now know which answer is which.

And let me deepen the memory picture too, with the contrast that finally made it click for a student of mine some years ago. Compare a photograph album with a pair of hands. The album stores: every picture is in there, findable, pointable, and if a picture was never taken, the album has nothing to say about that day. The hands embody: no job is stored in them, yet everything about how they move was written by the jobs, and they can handle a job they have never done before by drawing on the shape of all the jobs they have. A model is hands, not album. I keep returning to this because nearly every wrong expectation I correct in this field is an album expectation brought to a hands system. People expect recall and get judgement. They expect evidence and get conclusions. They expect the system to know what it has seen and admit what it has not, and the system can do neither, because nothing in it is stored as a seen thing. Expect hands, and the behaviour makes sense: brilliant on familiar ground, inventive on nearby ground, quietly unreliable on ground its experience never touched, and never, ever able to show you the album. There is no album. There was never an album. There are only the settings, shaped by the weather of the examples.

One more walk through the title, then, with both halves lit. A function with a memory of examples. The function half tells you the mechanics: inputs in, outputs out, the settings deciding. The memory half tells you the biography: those settings carry the shape of every example the function was trained on, the way your own judgement carries the shape of every client you have ever served. And the two halves together tell you the limit: the function can only output what its memory of examples has prepared it to output. It has no other resources. It cannot consult the world, it cannot reason its way back to first principles, it cannot notice that today is a strange day unlike its examples, unless strangeness itself was in the examples with labels attached. Everything a model does, it does out of its past. That is why the past you feed a system, if you ever feed one, is the most consequential decision in the whole arrangement, and why lesson two's warning about garbage will echo through this entire department. The model is its training, remembered as shape. There is nothing else in the box. I keep saying there is nothing else in the box, and I will keep saying it, because the day that sentence feels obvious to you is the day the fog has fully left the room.

Let me also say a word about size, since model sizes are quoted at buyers like engine sizes at car lots, and the comparison deserves an honest frame. A larger model, more parameters, more examples, longer training, can hold finer distinctions and more of them, the way a bigger workshop with more specialised tools can take on finer work. That is real, and for some jobs it is decisive. But size is not a synonym for fit. A vast model trained on the general internet knows the general shape of business writing; a small model trained on your two years of sent emails knows you. For the job of sounding like you, the small one can win, and it will cost less, run faster, and fail in ways you can predict. The fog move is to sell size as quality itself. The clear move is to ask: fit for which job, trained on whose examples, at what cost per use. A model is a function with a memory of examples, and the first question about any memory is never how big it is. It is what it is a memory of.

One last illustration, and I choose it from the biggest member of the family, because if the definition holds for the biggest member it holds for all of them. Consider the chatbot, the system that drafts, answers, summarises, and converses, the one most likely to be described to you as a mind. Run it through today's lens and watch what survives. Is it a function? Yes, precisely: the conversation so far goes in, and the next words come out, and it does this one stretch of words at a time, each new stretch a fresh run of the same function on a longer input. Are its settings a memory of examples? Yes: it was trained on an enormous body of text, and everything fluent in it, every rhythm of explanation, every shape of an apology or a sales letter or a condolence note, is the shape of that text settled into numbers. Can it show you its evidence? No: it can produce more words, some of which will sound like evidence, and the difference between evidence and words that sound like evidence is a difference you must supply, because the function cannot. Can it generalise? Beautifully, within the world its examples described, and that world is wide, which is why the system feels wide. And can it step outside that world? No more than your hands can perform a job no job prepared them for. That is the largest, most impressive system in the field, described completely by a sentence from a fundamentals course: a function with a memory of examples. If the sentence feels too small for the system, sit with that feeling a moment. The feeling is the fog leaving. The system did not shrink. Your description of it became exact, and exact descriptions always feel smaller than foggy ones, the way a map feels smaller than the mystery of an unmapped coast. The coast is the same size it always was. Now you can sail it.

And a short word about trust, since a definition that cannot guide trust is only a slogan. You now know what kind of trust a model has earned when it has earned any: the trust you give a trained pair of hands. You trust them on the work they were trained on, you watch them on work near the edge of it, and you do not hand them work from a different trade entirely and act surprised. You also know how such trust is checked: not by asking the hands to explain themselves, which they cannot do, but by watching their outputs on cases where you already know the answer. Every serious evaluation of a model works exactly like that, whatever it is called in the brochure: held-back examples, known answers, counted errors. When you test a tool on twenty of your own past enquiries before letting it near a live one, you are not doing a crude version of the science. You are doing the science, at the scale your business needs. The definition told you how. That is what definitions are for.

And if you remember nothing else from today, remember the posture this definition gives you in a negotiation. When someone presents a model to you now, you are no longer looking at a marvel or a threat. You are looking at a function, and you can ask function questions: what goes in, what comes out, what was it trained on, where does its memory of examples run out. Four questions, all of them answerable by an honest seller, none of them answerable by fog. That is the practical cash value of a definition, and it compounds across every purchase, every hire, and every headline from here on.

Recap, in order. First: a function is a machine for turning inputs into outputs, and a model is a function, nothing more mystical and nothing less useful. Second: what makes a model different from a designed function is that its behaviour was grown, not written: its parameters were adjusted over examples until its guesses became good. Third: its memory of examples is embodied, not stored: the examples survive as the shape of the settings, the way a riverbed remembers floods and hands remember work. Fourth: because the memory is shape rather than items, a model can generalise to cases it has never seen, and for the same reason it cannot show you its evidence or hand you a receipt. Fifth: this class's set problem stands on six bones — function, inputs, outputs, parameters, examples, predictions — plus one honest example from your own life where prediction, not understanding, was enough. Sixth: keep the layers apart — model, product, and machine are three different things, and judging them separately is what clear thinking looks like in this field.

What comes next is the questions on this lesson, with the full text open beside you, as always; going back to read is learning, not cheating, and the set problem's shape is worth a second look before you answer. When you are done, lesson four takes the output side of everything we have built and slows down on it: prediction as the core act, the one move every member of the family is making, in the workshop and in the wild. You came in today with ingredients. You leave with the thing itself. That was the whole point of lesson three.
