lessons.title: Prediction as the core act
paragraphs: Come in. I am Professor David Kim, and this is AI Fundamentals, lesson four. We have built the machine piece by piece: the name cleared in lesson one, the three ingredients counted in lesson two, the model itself defined in lesson three as a function with a memory of examples. Today we watch the machine do its one and only trick, and we give that trick its proper name. The name is prediction, and my claim for this lesson, which I will spend our time together proving, is that prediction is the core act: the single move underneath every member of the family, from the spam filter to the chatbot to the thing that decides who sees your advertisements. Two acts, and the whole class turns on keeping them apart. Training is the showing: before the system ever meets you, its settings are adjusted over millions of examples. Prediction is the act: afterwards, one new case at a time, the system produces its guess. Training happens in the workshop. Prediction happens in the wild. By the end of this lesson you will be able to take any AI system doing anything at all and find the prediction inside it, the way you can find the engine inside any car once someone has shown you what an engine looks like. That skill is worth money to you, because a person who can find the prediction can ask how good the prediction is, and that question, asked calmly and repeatedly, is the most powerful question a buyer owns.

Let us define prediction the way this room defines everything: plainly, and smaller than the fog wants it. A prediction is a guess about something not yet known, produced from patterns in things already known. Notice the parts. There is a guess, which means it can be wrong, and any system whose output cannot be wrong is not predicting, it is looking something up. There is something not yet known: the future, most obviously, but also the present you have not checked and the past nobody recorded. Your spam filter predicts something about the present: this message, which no human has judged yet, belongs in the junk folder. That is a prediction even though nothing about it is in the future, because the answer is unknown at the moment the guess is made and the guess is made from patterns, not from a lookup. And there is the basis: patterns in things already known, the examples, the memory of examples from lesson three. A prediction is the memory of examples, pointed at a new case. That is the whole act. Everything else is costume.

Now let me prove the claim by walking the family, the way we did in lesson one, and finding the prediction inside each member with the lights on. The sorter first, because it hides the prediction best. Sorting feels like knowing: the filter does not say this message might be junk, it simply moves it, decisively, the way a clerk files a letter. But the decisiveness is a costume too. Underneath, the filter predicted: shown this message, the pattern of its settings says junk is the likely verdict, likely enough to act on. Sorting is prediction with the uncertainty trimmed off for display, and once you see that, you will ask the sorter the predictor's question: how often is the sort wrong, and wrong in which direction, because a real enquiry filed as junk costs you a client and a junk message filed as real costs you a glance, and those are not the same cost, and a good buyer weighs them differently. The predictor member wears the act openly: the map predicting your arrival, the tool predicting which client will need you again. Nothing to uncover there, except to notice that it is the same act as the sorter's, with the uncertainty left visible. The recommender is a predictor working a crowd: for each person and each post, it predicts attention, will this one linger, and it shows the post where the predicted lingering is highest. Your reach, as a marketer, is a field of other people's predictions about attention, and I do not think that sentence can be repeated too often in a marketing company. And the maker, the generator, the chatbot, the member that feels least like a guesser: it is a predictor running in a loop. It predicts the next word. Then it predicts the next word after that, given the words so far, including its own. Then the next. A paragraph is hundreds of predictions in a row, each one small, each one shaped by the memory of examples, and the fluency that feels like thought is what you get when the small predictions are very good and very fast. The image makers work the same way in their own medium: prediction, in strokes and patches, all the way down. Four members, one act. I told you in lesson one that the shape never changes: something goes in, a guess comes out. Today the guess has its name. It is a prediction, every time, in every member, without exception.

There is a technical word for the act that you will meet in documentation and in sales material, and I want you to own it rather than be impressed by it: inference. When engineers say a model is running inference, they mean the model is being used: a new case is going through the frozen settings and a prediction is coming out. Inference is prediction, wearing its work clothes. The pair is worth fixing side by side: training is the showing, inference is the using. Training happens in the workshop, before the system meets you, at enormous expense, over millions of examples. Inference happens in the wild, after, cheaply, one case at a time, millions of times a day across the world. When a vendor's page boasts about their inference speed or their inference cost, they are talking about how fast and how cheaply the frozen model produces predictions, and now the boast is legible to you as a plain business fact rather than a spell. Words stop being fog the moment you can translate them on sight, and inference is one of the words this course exists to defog.

Now, the timeline, because keeping the two acts apart in time is the practical skill inside this lesson. Lay it on a timeline. On the left, the long before: millions of examples, settings adjusted again and again, the workshop lit for weeks. That is training. On the right, the quick after: one fresh case arrives, and out comes a guess, in a fraction of a second, for a fraction of a cent. That is prediction. Before and after; workshop and wild. The reason I press this so hard is that the two acts are constantly being blurred in conversation, usually in one specific direction: the system is described as learning from you while you use it. For the overwhelming majority of systems you will ever touch, that is not happening. Your corrections, your clever prompts, your frustrated rephrasings: they shape the current conversation, because the conversation is part of the input, but they do not retrain the model. The settings are frozen. The workshop is elsewhere and elsewhen. What feels like the system learning you is the system predicting with more of your words in its input, which is a real and useful thing, and a different thing. Why does the difference matter to a business owner? Because it tells you where improvement comes from. If a tool's predictions about your clients are poor, the fix is not to be patient with it while it learns you. The fix is better examples in its next training, or a different tool, or your own judgement on top. Patience is a virtue in many places. Waiting for a frozen function to thaw itself is not one of them.

Let us talk about how good a prediction is, because prediction has a beautiful property that understanding does not: it can be graded. A prediction is a guess about something that will become known, or can be checked, and when it becomes known you can count. The filter predicted junk; was it junk? The tool predicted this client would return; did she? Count the hits, count the misses, and you have the beginning of knowledge about a system, real knowledge, the kind you can take to a bank. This is why I keep steering you toward prediction language and away from understanding language. Understanding cannot be graded. There is no scoreboard for whether a chatbot truly grasps your brand. But its predictions can be graded, every one of them, and a vendor who believes in his system will help you grade it, and a vendor who steers you back to words like understands and knows is steering you away from the scoreboard. Insist on the scoreboard. Keep your own, in a notebook if you must: what the tool predicted, what actually happened, twenty cases, fifty. You will learn more about any system from fifty graded predictions than from fifty pages of its marketing, and you will learn it in the only currency that matters, which is what happens next in your actual business.

One refinement belongs here, because predictions are not all built the same and the difference shows up in how you should use them. Some predictions come as a verdict: junk, not junk; call her, do not call her. Others come as a likelihood: a seventy percent chance this enquiry becomes a client, a thirty percent chance of rain on the day of the shoot. The likelihood kind is more honest and more useful, because it tells you how to bet your time. A seventy percent enquiry deserves your first call of the morning. A thirty percent enquiry deserves a call too, perhaps, but not the first one, and not at the price of the seventy. Trouble begins when a likelihood is dressed as a verdict, when a tool shows you only its top guess and hides how close the second guess was. Two enquiries can both be labelled promising while one sits at ninety percent and the other at fifty-one, and they should not be worked the same way. So here is a buyer's habit to take from this lesson: whenever a tool gives you a verdict, ask what the likelihood was, and whenever it gives you a likelihood, ask what it was graded against. The systems that can answer both questions are the systems built by people who grade themselves. The others are asking you to grade them as magic, and we settled what to do with magic in lesson one.

Now the guided try-it, because this act of finding the prediction should be practised while I am here to practise it with you. I will name three things tools do in a marketing week, and for each one I want you to say, in a full sentence, what is being predicted, from what patterns, about what unknown. First: the tool drafts your advertisement. Say it with me. The system predicts, word by word, the words most likely to follow the words so far, from patterns in an enormous memory of examples of writing, about the unknown of what text should come next. The draft is a prediction of text. Second: the tool tells you Tuesday at ten is the best time to post. The system predicts the attention your post will receive at each possible time, from patterns in past posts and their results, about the unknown of how this post will do. The schedule is a prediction of attention. Third, and this one is the quietest: the tool summarises a long email thread for you. The system predicts the words of a shorter text that patterns say belong with threads like this one, about the unknown of what a good summary here would say. Even summarising, which feels like pure understanding, is prediction underneath: a guess at the words, checkable against the thread, gradable by you in ten seconds. Run that sentence shape over anything a tool does this week: the system predicts this, from patterns in that, about this unknown. When you can fill in all three blanks, the tool has no fog left to hide in. When you cannot fill in the middle blank, the patterns, you have found the exact question to ask its seller.

Before the recap, let me show you grading done once, in full, on numbers small enough to hold in your head, because I want the scoreboard to be a thing you have seen and not just a metaphor I praise. Imagine you let a tool rank your enquiries for one month, and you write down its top prediction each time: this one will become a client. Say it makes that call on twenty enquiries. The month ends. You count. Fourteen of the twenty became clients. Six did not. Now you know something no brochure could tell you: on your enquiries, in your town, in your trade, this tool's top prediction was right fourteen times out of twenty. And the counting teaches you more the longer you keep it, because you can start asking the second-order questions. Of the six misses, were they all one kind of enquiry, say the ones from outside your area? Then the tool has a blind spot with an address, and you can compensate for it yourself, which is what a good owner does with any employee's weakness. Of the clients you actually won that month, how many did the tool rank low? That is the miss nobody notices, the false alarm's quiet twin, and it matters because a tool that only confirms the obvious is furniture, not help. Notice what made all of this possible: the predictions were written down before the outcomes were known. A prediction remembered afterwards is not a prediction; it is a story, and stories always grade themselves kindly. Write it down, date it, count it later. That humble discipline, applied to machines, is the entire scientific method of this field wearing work boots, and it is available to you tonight with a notebook and a pencil.

Why does prediction work at all? It is worth one honest minute, because the answer explains both the power you have seen and the brittleness waiting in lesson five. Prediction works because the world has habits. People who ask about price in the first line usually keep asking about price. Messages shaped like past junk are usually junk. Attention gathers where attention gathered before. The patterns in the examples are not arbitrary; they are the fingerprints of those habits, and a model is, in the end, a very large collection of the world's habits, distilled into settings. But habits are not laws. Habits shift: a competitor opens across town, a platform changes what it rewards, a phrase that worked all spring tires out by autumn, and the world's new behaviour no longer matches the habits in the frozen settings. The model cannot notice. Noticing was never installed. It will keep predicting the old world with undiminished confidence, and the scoreboard, your scoreboard, is the only instrument that will register the change. This is why grading is not a one-time inspection you perform at purchase. It is a habit of your own, the owner's habit, matching the machine's habits, and the day your counts start slipping is the day you have learned something worth real money: the world moved, and the frozen function did not.

One more subtlety, and it is the subtlest thing in this lesson, so take it slowly. Some predictions change the thing they predict. When the recommender predicts you will linger on a certain kind of post and therefore shows you more of that kind, your lingering is partly the prediction's own doing: the guess helped make itself true. When a tool predicts an enquiry is promising and you therefore answer it within the hour, warmly, with your best attention, while the low-ranked enquiry waits two days for a cooler reply, the outcomes at month's end are partly your doing, downstream of the ranking. The scoreboard still matters, more than ever, but read it with this in mind: a prediction handed to a person who acts on it is not a weather forecast. It is more like a coach's call, entangled with the playing of the game. This is not a reason to distrust the act. It is a reason to keep your own judgement in the loop, visibly, especially where your actions are the mechanism by which predictions come true or false. The owner who knows he is part of the system grades more honestly than the owner who thinks he is only watching it.

And a word about causation, briefly, because prediction's oldest trap lives there. A model finds that enquiries mentioning a deadline become clients. It does not find, and cannot find, whether the deadline causes the seriousness, or whether serious people simply mention deadlines, or whether some third thing produces both. For prediction, the difference does not matter: the pattern pays either way. But the moment you act on a pattern as if it were a cause, the difference can cost you. If you instructed every client to mention a deadline, you would not manufacture seriousness; you would manufacture deadlines. Patterns tell you what travels together. They are silent about what produces what. Keep prediction for prediction's jobs — ranking, sorting, drafting, timing — and bring causes in only where you have evidence of the slower, human kind. That sentence will save you from the most respectable-looking mistake in the whole field, which is steering a business by correlations as if they were levers.

Let me also place prediction beside its neighbours, because three words get traded for one another in sales talk and they are not the same. A lookup finds a stored answer: your calendar lookup does not predict your Thursday appointment, it retrieves it, and it is never wrong in the prediction way, only out of date. A calculation derives an answer from rules: the invoice total is calculated, and if the rules and the inputs are right, the total is right with a certainty no prediction ever earns. A prediction guesses an unknown from patterns, and it carries its error rate with it like a shadow, always, even when the shadow is small. Systems get sold by borrowing the dignity of the neighbours: the prediction is presented with the confidence of a calculation, or the finality of a lookup. Your defence is classification. When a tool speaks, ask which of the three it just did. If it predicted, where is the error rate? If it calculated, what were the rules? If it looked something up, how fresh is the store? Three kinds of answer, three kinds of trust, and a great deal of expensive confusion dissolves the moment you refuse to let one kind wear another's clothes.

And since this lesson is the heart of the course, I will say its heart out loud once more, in the plainest form I own. You do not need these systems to be minds. You need them to be right often enough, on the cases you feed them, at a cost below the value of being right. Prediction is the act that can be measured against that standard, which is why this course keeps returning to it the way a compass needle returns north. Understanding is a beautiful word and a genuine mystery, and it is somebody else's course. This one is about machinery that guesses from examples, and the guessing, graded honestly, is more than enough to build on. Hold the standard — right often enough, on your cases, at the right cost — and every tool you meet from now on walks up to the same measuring wall.

One more scene from your week, to fix the timeline in muscle memory, and then we recap. Picture the morning you first use a new drafting tool. You type a client's situation, and out comes a reply in something like your voice. It feels, irresistibly, as though the tool has come to know you in the last ten minutes. Run the timeline over that feeling. The knowing, such as it is, happened months ago and miles away, in the workshop, when the settings were adjusted over millions of examples of writing, very few of them yours. This morning's event is on the right side of the timeline: one fresh case, your words, run through frozen settings, one prediction out. The feeling of being known is the prediction's fluency wearing the costume of acquaintance. None of this makes the draft worse. It may be an excellent draft. But if you believe the tool has learned you this morning, you will make two mistakes: you will trust tomorrow's draft more than today's evidence warrants, because surely it knows you better now, and you will blame yourself when it errs, as though you had taught it badly. Both mistakes dissolve under the timeline. The settings were frozen before you arrived. Your job is not to teach the tool. Your job is to grade its predictions and to bring your own knowledge, the real, accumulated, understanding kind, to the cases where the pattern runs out. That division of labour, machine predicts and owner judges, is the working heart of every good arrangement I have seen between a business and these systems, and it is the arrangement this whole course is quietly training you to run.

And a final distinction for the road, small in words and large in consequence: the difference between a prediction and a promise. A promise binds the speaker. When you tell a client the work will be done by Friday, you have not merely guessed about Friday; you have committed yourself to making Friday true, and your honour is the mechanism. A model's prediction binds nothing and commits nothing. It is a reading of patterns, offered without stake. The trouble, and I have watched this trouble cost real money, is that fluent predictions are easily heard as promises, by customers, by staff, and by owners at the end of a long day. A delivery date a tool suggested, repeated to a client, becomes the client's expectation and your obligation, while the tool's part in it evaporates. So handle predictions the way a careful person handles a talented but unaccountable adviser's tips: write them down as predictions, grade them as predictions, and convert them into promises only through your own judgement, at the moment you choose, knowing the obligation is yours alone. The machine guesses. The owner promises. Keeping those two verbs with their rightful owners is most of professional maturity in the age of this machinery, and you are nearly trained in it already.

If you take one habit from this lesson into the rest of your education, let it be the habit of writing predictions down before outcomes arrive, for machines and for people alike, including yourself. Your own gut predictions about clients, campaigns, and hires are also guesses from patterns, the patterns of your experience, and they deserve the same honest grading you now give the machine's. Owners who grade their own calls get sharper. Owners who remember their calls kindly stay exactly as sharp as they were. The scoreboard does not care whose prediction it grades, and that impartiality is its kindness.

Carry the timeline in your pocket this week and lay every claim you hear across it, left side or right side, workshop or wild, and you will find that half the confusion in any conversation about this technology is simply the two acts being traded mid-sentence by people who never separated them.

Recap, in order. First: prediction is the core act, a guess about something not yet known, produced from patterns in things already known, and every member of the family, sorter, predictor, recommender, and maker, is performing it. Second: sorting is prediction with the uncertainty trimmed off, and making is prediction running in a loop, one next word at a time. Third: inference is the engineer's word for the same act, the using of the frozen model, as training is the showing that froze it. Fourth: the two acts live on a timeline, training in the workshop, long and expensive, before; prediction in the wild, quick and cheap, after, and most systems do not learn from you while you use them. Fifth: predictions can be graded and understandings cannot, so insist on the scoreboard, count hits and misses on your own cases, and prefer likelihoods you can bet your morning on over verdicts that hide how close the call was.

What comes next is the questions on this lesson, and as always the full text stays open beside them; going back to read is learning, not cheating, and the sentence shape from our try-it is worth keeping in front of you while you answer. When you are done, lesson five takes the graded scoreboard seriously and asks the honest question: where is all this prediction strong, where is it brittle, and why are both true of the same machine at the same time. You now know the one act. Next we map where the act holds and where it cracks.

lessons.title: Where AI is strong, where it is brittle, and why
paragraphs: Come in. I am Professor David Kim, and this is AI Fundamentals, lesson five. You now know what the machinery is, what it is made of, what a model is, and what act it performs. Today we grade it. The title of the lesson is the whole agenda: where AI is strong, where it is brittle, and why both are true of the same machine at the same time. This is the lesson the salesmen hope you skip, and it is also the lesson the fear merchants hope you skip, because both of them need a one-sided picture and the truth here is two-sided in a very specific, very learnable way. The strengths are real, and I will state them at full size. The brittleness is real, and I will state it at full size too. And the why, the single design fact that produces both lists, is something you already know: a model is a function with a memory of examples, and everything in today's lesson is that sentence, cashed out. By the end you will be able to look at any task in your business and sort it, calmly, into work this machinery should do, work it should do with you watching, and work it should never touch. That sorting is the most valuable skill in this course for a working owner, and it cannot be bought as a feature. It can only be learned. Let us learn it.

The strengths first, at full size, because a fog-clearer does not minimise. Strength one: scale of experience. A trained model carries the distilled shape of more examples than any human being will meet in a lifetime. You have read perhaps a few thousand business emails closely in your life. A writing model has been shaped by more text than a thousand lifetimes of reading. On any task where the pattern lives in volume, the machine starts with an advantage no hiring decision can match. Strength two: speed. A prediction takes a fraction of a second. The model can sort a thousand enquiries, draft a hundred routine replies, and scan a year of reviews for recurring complaints in the time it takes you to drink your coffee, and the thousandth prediction is made with the same care as the first. Strength three, the twin of speed: tirelessness. The model does not get bored at hour six. It does not skim the last fifty invoices because the first fifty were dull. A great deal of expensive human error is fatigue error, and this machinery simply does not have that failure mode. Strength four: consistency. Given the same patterns, it reaches for the same judgements, Monday and Friday, in January and in June, unaffected by mood, weather, or a difficult morning. And strength five, the one I find genuinely remarkable: breadth of pattern. Because the examples span so much, the model sometimes connects things no single specialist would connect, a phrasing from one trade that unlocks a problem in another, a structure from one kind of document that organises a different kind. That breadth is the source of the moments that make people say the word creative about these systems, and while I will keep correcting the word, I will not correct the moment away. The moments are real. On familiar ground, at volume, under time pressure, with patterns that live in examples: this machinery is strong in ways that should change how a small company is run, and a competitor who understands that is dangerous to one who does not.

Now the brittleness, at the same size, in the same plain voice. Brittle point one, and it is the master key to all the others: the model knows only its examples, and it does not know what it does not know. Inside the territory its training covered thickly, its predictions are usually good. Step outside that territory, into the unusual client, the unprecedented situation, the week the world changed, and the predictions can be wild, and they arrive in exactly the same confident shape as the good ones. The system has no edge detector. It cannot feel the ground thinning under its feet, because feeling the ground was never part of the design. Brittle point two: fluency outruns accuracy. The language models in particular produce sentences whose smoothness is not evidence about their truth. A draft can read beautifully and contain a wrong date, an invented discount, a promise you never made, a fact about your own business that is simply not so, stated in your own voice, better than you would have stated it. The field has a word for the system inventing things in this fluent way, and you should know the word because you will meet it: hallucination. Strip the costume and it is exactly what this course would predict. A machine that produces the next likely words will, when the true words are not in its patterns, produce likely words instead, and likely words are sometimes invented ones. It is not lying. Lying requires knowing the truth and choosing otherwise. It is guessing past the edge of its memory and not knowing it has crossed the edge, which in some ways is more dangerous, because there is no malice to detect, only confidence to discount. Brittle point three: no stake and no world. The model does not live with the consequences of its predictions. It does not meet the client whose quote was wrong. It does not know that your town's big employer just announced layoffs, unless that fact is in its input, because it has no window and no ears; its world is its examples and the text you hand it, full stop. And brittle point four: frozenness. The settings were set in the workshop at a moment in the past. Prices change, platforms change, your own offers change, and the model goes on predicting the world as its examples described it, until somebody retrains it. Every one of these four points, notice, is the strength list read from the other side. Tireless consistency is frozenness that cannot adapt. Breadth of pattern is a memory that cannot tell its centre from its edge. Fluency is prediction doing its job so well that it predicts straight past the truth. One design, two faces. That is the why, and if you remember nothing else today, remember that the strengths and the brittleness are not two facts about the machine. They are one fact, seen from two sides.

Let me make the sorting skill concrete with your own week's work, because this is where the lesson earns its keep. Into the first pile, work the machinery should simply do: sorting and filing, first drafts of routine messages, summarising long threads for your eyes only, finding the recurring phrases in a hundred reviews, turning your spoken notes into tidy text, suggesting posting times, ranking enquiries for your attention. What do these share? The patterns are thick, the volume is high, the cost of a single error is small, and you will see the output before the world does. Into the second pile, work it should do with you watching: drafts of anything a client will read under your name, prices suggested but not sent, replies to complaints, anything involving a date, a figure, or a commitment. The machinery drafts, you grade, you send. Your judgement is the edge detector the system does not have, and on this pile your job title is exactly that. Into the third pile, work it should never touch alone: anything where an error is expensive or irreversible, anything legal, medical, or financial in its consequences, anything depending on facts about your town this month that cannot be in its examples, and anything where the person on the other end needs, and deserves, a human being who will live with the outcome. The piles are not about trusting or distrusting the technology. They are about matching the task's shape to the machine's shape: thick patterns and cheap errors on one side, thin patterns and dear errors on the other, and your attention spread accordingly. An owner who sorts this way gets the speed without the scars.

Now our guided try-it, and I want you to actually run it, because sorting is a motor skill as much as an idea. I will name six tasks, quickly, and you call the pile before I do. A tool offers to answer your most common customer questions automatically, from your past answers. Pile two, shading toward one: the patterns are thick, they are your own answers, but the words go out under your name, so you watch until your scoreboard says otherwise. A tool offers to write the first version of your monthly newsletter. Pile one for the draft, pile two for the send, and notice how many real tasks split exactly like that, draft and send in different piles. A tool offers to predict which of your services will grow next year. Pile two at best, and handle with tongs: the patterns are thin, the world moves, and the prediction is a prompt for your thinking, never a substitute for it. A tool offers to handle a furious customer's complaint end to end while you are on holiday. Pile three. The patterns of fury are exactly where a memory of examples is weakest, the cost of a wrong tone is a reputation, and the customer deserves a person. A tool offers to pull every phone number and date out of a stack of documents into a tidy list. Pile one, with a spot check: extraction from thick patterns, errors cheap and visible. And a tool offers to tell you what a competitor across town charged a specific client last month. Pile three, and walk away from the tool as well: that fact is not in any legitimate examples, so whatever it answers is invention wearing a uniform, and now you can see the uniform for what it is. Six tasks, sorted. Run that drill on every new offer you receive and the offers will start sorting themselves.

Let me slow down on the strengths once more, with scenes, because a strength you have watched working is a strength you will actually use, and unused strengths are just brochure copy. Scene one: the Monday morning inbox of a company that has had a busy weekend. Ninety messages: enquiries, invoices, two complaints, a supplier changing terms, a dozen pieces of junk that slipped past the filter, and the one message that matters most, a client ready to sign, buried in the middle. A person needs an hour and a strong coffee to find the shape of that inbox, and by message seventy the skimming has begun and the skimming is where the signing client gets a slow reply. The machinery reads all ninety with the same attention, ranks them by the patterns of your past Mondays, and puts the signing client on top in seconds. That is scale, speed, and tirelessness not as abstractions but as a client answered while he was still warm. Scene two: a year of customer reviews, four hundred of them, which no owner will ever sit down and read end to end. The machinery can, and it finds that one phrase, parking, appears in a third of the unhappy ones, a pattern invisible to anyone reading a review at a time because no single review is about parking. Your business has a parking problem it did not know it had, found by breadth of pattern across volume no human would process. Scene three: the routine acknowledgement messages, the thank-you-for-your-enquiry notes that must go out fast, in your voice, forty times a month. Drafted by the machinery, glanced at by you, sent in minutes. Nobody's genius was needed for those messages. Somebody's hours were being spent on them, though, and now those hours belong to work that actually needs a mind. Hold those three scenes when the brittleness list starts to sour you on the whole enterprise. The strengths pay rent. That is why we bother mapping the cracks at all: not to discard the tool, but to use a rent-paying tool without letting it sign your name to its guesses.

And now the brittleness deserves the same treatment, scenes and all, because a crack you have watched opening is a crack you will spot in the wild. Scene one: the confident quote. An owner lets a tool draft a reply to a price enquiry, and the draft, fluent and warm, quotes a figure from a package the company stopped offering last spring. The settings were frozen before the spring. The tool does not know the offer died, because knowing things like that is not in its design; it predicted the words a reply like this usually contains, and the usual words carried the usual price. Caught by the owner at the watching pile, it is a funny story. Sent unwatched, it is a promise the company must honour or explain, and the explanation sounds exactly as good as it is. Scene two: the invented reference. A tool drafting a proposal mentions, helpfully, a project your company completed for a named business in a neighbouring town. The project does not exist. The business does, which makes it worse. The model needed a reference-shaped sentence, its patterns supplied one, and the sentence was smooth enough to sail past a tired reader. This is hallucination in working clothes: not exotic, not rare, and entirely predictable once you know the machine predicts words rather than checking facts. Scene three: the strange week. A storm, a road closure, a local factory's announcement, and suddenly the enquiries arriving are unlike any in the examples: urgent, confused, asking about things your company has never sold. The machinery ranks them by the old patterns, confidently, wrongly, and the owner who trusts the ranking that week answers the wrong people first. Nothing in the system announced that the world had moved. Systems like this never announce it. The announcement is your job, and it is made of local knowledge no model has: you live in the town the model only has examples of. Three scenes, one moral: the brittleness is not random malfunction. It is the design, meeting the edge of its examples, in a confident voice. Expect it there, specifically there, and it loses most of its power to harm you.

Fairness requires one more scene, on the other side of the ledger, and I will not skip it, because this room deals in full pictures. Human beings are brittle too, in our own well-documented ways. We get tired, we play favourites, we remember the last client and forget the forty before him, we are confident about things we half-read, and we invent, fluently and with total sincerity, when our memory runs out; the word confabulation exists in psychology for a reason. The honest comparison is not machine brittle, human solid. It is two different brittlenesses, with different shapes. Human error tends to be noisy and self-doubting at the edges; we hesitate, we say I am not sure, we go and check, because we live in the world the answer is about and the world pushes back on us. Machine error tends to be smooth and certain at the edges, because nothing pushes back inside the settings. That difference is why the partnership works when it is arranged properly: the machine supplies the scale and the stamina, the human supplies the doubt and the world. Arrange it the other way, human doing volume until fatigue makes the errors, machine supplying unexamined certainty on top, and you have built the worst of both. The three piles from earlier are exactly this partnership, written as a work rota. That is all they ever were.

So the why, one final time, stated as a single chain you can recite. The model is a function. Its settings are a memory of examples. Prediction is running new cases through that memory. Therefore the model is strong wherever the new cases resemble the remembered ones, because the memory is vast, fast, and tireless. Therefore it is brittle wherever the new cases depart from the remembered ones, because there is nothing else in the box to consult: no world, no doubt, no stake, no clock. Strength and brittleness are not a balance the engineers struck. They are the same property, resemblance, helping you on one side of the line and leaving you on the other. And the line itself is invisible to the machine, which is the single most important sentence in this lesson, and I will repeat it in different words so it has two chances to stay with you: the system cannot tell you where its own competence ends. You are the boundary detector. In every arrangement you build with this technology, for the rest of your working life, that is the job that remains yours, and no release note will ever retire you from it.

A few working habits grow directly out of today's map, and I want them named before we close, because a map nobody acts on is decoration. Habit one: spot-check the strong pile. Even work the machinery does alone gets sampled by your eyes, a few outputs a week, the way a good owner walks a floor he trusts. The sampling is not distrust. It is how you notice the world moving before the errors get expensive. Habit two: keep the scoreboard from lesson four running on the watched pile, and let it promote and demote tasks between piles. A drafting tool that grades well for three months on your cases earns more freedom. One that invents a second date earns less. The piles are not commandments; they are a living rota, revised by evidence, which is the most this-course sentence I can offer you. Habit three: never let a fluent output skip the check on its checkable parts. Dates, figures, names, prices, and promises are the five things to verify in any draft before it leaves, because those are the places where a predicted word and a true word part company most expensively. Read the warmth of the draft for tone if you like; then read those five things like an auditor. Habit four: write down the strange weeks. When the world moves, a storm, a closure, a sudden change in your market, note it in the same notebook as your scoreboard, because a dip in the machine's grading that matches a note in your book is not a mystery; it is the boundary, found and marked, and marked boundaries are how an owner learns the true shape of a tool's territory faster than any manual could teach it.

And let me close the teaching by returning the lesson to its proper emotional temperature, because I have heard this material land two wrong ways and I want neither for you. It should not land as fear: nothing in the brittleness list is a reason to refuse the strengths, any more than a car's ability to leave the road is a reason to walk everywhere. It should not land as complacency either: nothing in the strengths list licenses an unwatched signature. It should land as professionalism, the calm of a person who knows a tool's working range the way a carpenter knows a saw's. Every powerful tool has a range. Inside it, the work sings. Outside it, the same power that made the work sing makes the damage fast. Knowing the range is not a limitation on your ambition. It is what separates the owner who will still be profiting from this machinery in ten years from the one who will be telling a story about the winter it quoted the dead package to his best client. You are being trained for the ten-year version. That is the whole design of this course, and today was its most practical day.

One more distinction sharpens the whole map, and then we are done with the teaching. It is the difference between a mistake and a fabrication, because owners punish them as one thing and they are two. A mistake is a wrong prediction on a case inside the territory: the ranking put a weak enquiry above a strong one, the draft chose the second-best wording. Mistakes are the cost of prediction, they are counted by the scoreboard, and a good rate of them is the price of the speed. A fabrication is a prediction that sailed off the territory entirely and brought back an invented fact in a confident voice: the dead package's price, the project that never happened. Fabrications are not a worse grade of mistake; they are a different event, the boundary being crossed without a signal. The management differs accordingly. Mistakes you budget for. Fabrications you design against: the five-point check, the watched pile, the rule that names, dates, figures, prices, and promises are verified by a person before they travel. When you can say which of the two just happened in your business, and respond to each in its own way, you are no longer a user of this technology. You are its manager, which is the rank this course has been quietly promoting you to since lesson one.

Let me leave you a single question to carry out of this lesson, because it compresses the whole map into something you can ask in a doorway, in a sales meeting, in your own head at midnight. The question is: what would this look like if it were wrong? Ask it of a ranking and you remember to glance at the bottom of the list as well as the top. Ask it of a draft and your eyes go to the dates and the figures. Ask it of a confident summary and you open the original thread for the one paragraph that mattered. The question works because it points your attention at the boundary, which is where, as we have established at some length, all the interesting failures live and where the machine itself will never point. Tools that survive the question earn more of your business. Tools whose sellers flinch at it have told you which pile they belong in, and it is the third one, the one with the door that stays closed.

Let me also give you the buyer's version of this entire lesson, compressed into the three questions that belong in every demonstration you ever sit through, because a demonstration is a performance on the performer's home ground and the map tells you exactly how to take it off that ground. Question one: show me it failing. An honest builder can show you the kinds of cases where the system is weak, because he has graded them; a seller who claims there are none is telling you his system does not know what it does not know, and neither does he. Question two: show me it on my cases. Your enquiries, your reviews, your town, your spring prices — the territory is yours, and performance on the builder's territory is evidence about the builder's territory only. Question three: what happens when the world changes? The honest answer involves retraining, updating, and your own scoreboard catching the drift; the fog answer involves the system adapting, learning, and keeping up, verbs we have spent four lessons learning to translate. Three questions, each one a direct application of today's map, and together they will do more for your purchasing than any feature comparison ever printed. A tool is not strong or brittle in the abstract. It is strong or brittle on a territory, for a task, at a cost of error — and you are the only person in the room who knows your territory, your tasks, and your costs. That is why this lesson could not be replaced by a rating website. The map is general. The territory is yours.

Recap, in order. First: the strengths are scale of experience, speed, tirelessness, consistency, and breadth of pattern, and they are real and full-sized. Second: the brittleness is just as real: the model does not know what it does not know, its fluency outruns its accuracy and can invent in a confident voice, it has no stake and no window on the world, and its settings are frozen in the past. Third: the two lists are one fact, the memory of examples, seen from two sides, which is why no update will ever give you the strengths with the brittleness removed. Fourth: the owner's skill is sorting tasks into three piles, machinery alone, machinery watched, and machinery never, by asking two questions: how thick are the patterns, and how dear is an error.

What comes next is the questions on this lesson, with the full text open beside you, as always; going back to read is learning, not cheating. When you are done, lesson six, our last, gathers the whole course into the honest vocabulary: the words to use, the words to refuse, and the set problem one final time, in your own words, standing on everything we have built. You came in today with a machine. You leave knowing where it stands firm and where it cracks, and why. That is most of wisdom about any tool, and you have it now.

lessons.title: The honest vocabulary: no magic, no menace
paragraphs: Come in. I am Professor David Kim, and this is AI Fundamentals, lesson six, our last lesson together. Its title is the rule of this room, stated one final time: the honest vocabulary — no magic, no menace. Across five lessons we built the machinery in plain words. We named the thing in lesson one: programs that learn patterns from examples. We counted the ingredients in lesson two: data, parameters, training. We defined the product in lesson three: a model, a function with a memory of examples. We found the core act in lesson four: prediction, in the workshop and in the wild. And in lesson five we graded the whole arrangement: strong where the new cases resemble the remembered ones, brittle where they depart, one design with two faces. Today we do the thing all of that was for. We fix the words. Because a vocabulary is not decoration on knowledge; a vocabulary is where knowledge lives when it leaves the classroom and goes to work in your week. You will forget, in time, some of my sentences. You will not forget the words you reach for when a salesman smiles, a headline shouts, or a tool does something uncanny at midnight. If those words are honest ones, the knowledge is still working. If they are fog words, the knowledge is gone no matter how well you once understood it. That is why the last lesson of a fundamentals course is a lesson about language, and why I ask you to take it as seriously as any lesson before it. It is the lesson that keeps the other five.

Here is the honest vocabulary, the whole of it, laid out on the table the way we built it, one word at a time, with its plain meaning attached. Data: the examples the system learns from. Parameters: the internal settings inside it, the knobs. Training: the showing, the long process of adjusting those settings against the examples until the guesses come out right. Model: a function, a machine for turning inputs into outputs, whose settings were adjusted over examples until its predictions matched reality often enough to be useful. Prediction: the act itself, a guess about something not yet known, produced from patterns in things already known, one new case at a time. Inference: the same act in its work clothes, the using of the frozen model. And around those six, the honest adjectives: trained, frozen, graded, likely, brittle. A trained system, not a taught child. Frozen settings, not a growing mind. A graded prediction, with a scoreboard, not a trusted oracle. A likely outcome, with the likelihood stated, not a certain one. A brittle edge, named and watched, not a mysterious failure. Six nouns and a handful of honest adjectives: that is the entire vocabulary of this course, and I will tell you a secret about it. It is enough. Every true thing that can be said about the systems in this department can be said with those words, and every sentence about them that cannot survive translation into those words was never true to begin with. That is the test, and today we practise it until it is reflex.

Now the other list, the words to refuse, or at least to translate on sight, because each of them smuggles a mind into the box. The system knows. It does not know; it predicts from patterns, and the difference decides what questions you ask next. The system understands your brand. It does not understand; it was shown examples and its settings carry their shape, and the day your brand does something its examples never contained, the understanding will be nowhere to be found, because it was never there. The system thinks, decides, believes, wants, cares, creates. Each of those words names something a person does with a mind, and each of them, applied to the machinery, performs the same small theft: it moves your trust from the scoreboard, where it can be earned, to a character, where it can only be felt. I am not asking you to become a pedant, correcting your friends at dinner. I am asking you to run the translation in your own head, in the half second before you decide what something is worth. Knows becomes predicts from patterns in examples. Understands becomes was shaped by examples of. Decides becomes outputs the highest-ranked guess. Creates becomes generates, by predicting, in a loop, what usually comes next. The translation takes no time once it is habit, and it changes the temperature of every room it happens in, because fog cannot survive being translated out loud twice in a row.

And the two master fog words themselves, the pair in our title. Magic first. Magic is the word for a result whose workings we are not going to discuss. It is a curtain with a price tag. Whenever the workings of a system are hidden behind wonder, somebody is being protected from your questions, and it is not you. The honest vocabulary has no use for magic because the honest vocabulary is the workings: examples, settings, adjusting, guessing, grading. A thing explained is not diminished. The adjusted recipe is not less remarkable for our knowing it was adjusted. If anything the machinery is more impressive stated plainly, the way a bridge is more impressive when you understand the loads it carries than when you merely gasp at it. Then menace. Menace is the word for a result whose intentions we are invited to imagine. But the machinery has no intentions, and imagining them is the same curtain, hung from the other side. The real risks of these systems are not intentions and never were: they are the risks we mapped in lesson five, confident errors at the edge of the examples, invented facts in a fluent voice, frozen settings in a moving world, and owners who stopped grading because the outputs felt like a colleague's. Those risks are serious, manageable, and boring to headline, which is precisely why the headline prefers menace. No magic, no menace: not a slogan, a discipline. It means every claim about this technology gets translated into machinery before it gets believed, priced, or feared.

Let us now run the discipline at full speed, because our guided try-it today is the one I most want you to keep for the rest of your life: the headline drill. I will give you three headlines of the kind that will cross your phone this year, and we translate each one together, out loud, into the honest vocabulary, and then we judge what is left. Headline one: artificial intelligence now understands your customers better than you do. Translate. A model, trained on examples of customer behaviour, predicts some customer behaviour, on the cases resembling its examples, more accurately than an unaided owner. What is left after translation? Possibly a useful tool, and two questions: which behaviour, and graded how, on whose customers. The fog said better than you, full stop, a rival for your own knowledge of your own people. The translation says a predictor with a territory, which you can test this month for the price of a notebook. Headline two: the machine is learning, and soon it will not need us. Translate. The builders are training new versions of the model on new examples, in the workshop, as they have always done, and the frozen version in your hands is not learning anything tonight. What is left? A release schedule, dressed as an uprising. Headline three, my favourite, because it sounds so reasonable: our platform's intelligence makes the decisions, so you can relax. Translate. Our model ranks options by prediction and acts on the top-ranked guess without showing you the likelihood, the territory, or the scoreboard. What is left? An invitation to stop being the boundary detector, which lesson five identified as the one job that remains yours. Relax is the most expensive word in that headline. Three headlines, three translations, and notice: in every case the machinery underneath was worth taking seriously, and in every case the fog was the part asking for your money or your fear. The drill is the course. Everything before today was learning to do the drill.

And now, to close the course the way it deserves, we work the set problem one final time, in full, standing on everything we have built. The problem, as this course sets it: in your own words, one paragraph: what is a model, and what did training do to it? Use one example from your own life where prediction, not understanding, was enough. You heard my worked answer in lesson three, and you built your own with me there. Hear it once more, now with five lessons inside your ears, and notice how much more of it you can hear. A model is a function, a machine for turning inputs into outputs, whose internal settings were adjusted, over millions of examples, until its predictions matched reality often enough to be useful. Training is that adjustment. A spam filter never understood a word of your email; prediction was enough, and knowing the difference between the two is the whole first lesson. Six bones, as before: function, inputs, outputs, parameters, examples, predictions. But now you know what each bone carries. Function carries the shape of the act. Parameters carry the memory of examples, embodied, not stored. Training carries the workshop, the cost, the frozenness. Predictions carry the scoreboard, the likelihoods, the boundary you must detect. And the example carries the philosophy of the whole course: that prediction without understanding is not a scandal or a trick, but a working arrangement, powerful inside its territory and honest about what it is, as long as the human beside it keeps the vocabulary honest. When you write your own paragraph after this lesson, and I hope you will, write it as the owner you have become: machinery in plain words, an example from your own ground, and not one fog word standing.

There is a citizen's skill underneath all of this, and I named it in lesson one and I will name it again at the door: you will leave able to read any headline about AI and know, within a sentence or two, whether it is reporting or theatre. That skill now has a population of one more, and it matters beyond your purchasing, though it will save you money. It matters because this technology will be argued about, in public, by people selling wonder and people selling fear, for the rest of your life, and the arguments will be won by whoever controls the words. A person who says model, examples, settings, prediction, graded, brittle, in the right places, is a person whose neighbours can think clearly around them. Fog is contagious, and so is clarity. I have done my best to make you a carrier of the second. The rest of this department's classes, the ones about how machines learn in depth, about data and where it lives, about agents that act in the world, all of them assume the vocabulary you now own, and all of them will go faster for you because the fog cannot get a foothold. That is what a fundamentals course is for: not to finish your education, but to make the rest of it possible at speed.

Before the recap, let me hold a small clinic on the remaining everyday words, the ones too ordinary to have made the first list, because fog lives in ordinary words most comfortably of all. The system learns. This one is half honest, which makes it the most dangerous of the set. Training is a kind of learning, and I use the word myself about the workshop. But in the wild, at your desk, the frozen system is not learning, and the sentence the system learns from you, said by a seller, quietly promises that today's errors are tuition toward tomorrow's excellence. They are not. They are just today's errors. Translate: the system was trained, past tense, in the workshop, and the next version may be trained again. The system remembers. It carries a memory of examples, embodied in settings, and it remembers nothing about you, your last conversation, or Tuesday, unless those things are placed in its input again. Translate: the settings carry the shape of the training examples. The system sees your logo, reads your reviews, writes your posts. Sees, reads, writes: each word borrows a human act. The honest versions are longer and better: it processes an image and predicts what it depicts; it takes in text and predicts patterns in it; it generates text by predicting what usually comes next. Longer, yes. Fog is always shorter than honesty, which is exactly its commercial advantage, and why honesty has to be a practised discipline rather than a preference. And the word smart, which we met in lesson one: smart is a compliment wearing a lab coat. Translate it every time into the question it is dodging: good at what, on whose examples, graded how. A vocabulary is a set of questions as much as a set of answers, and the honest words are the ones that open questions while the fog words close them. Knows closes. Predicts opens: how often, on what, at whose expense. That difference, open versus closed, is the surest field test I can give you. When a word about this technology makes you feel that everything is settled, be suspicious. When it makes you ask the next question, keep it.

Now let me show you the vocabulary doing a full day's work, because words are only yours when you have watched them earn. Imagine you are writing the page on your own website that describes how your company uses these tools, and imagine writing it twice. First, the fog version, the version a thousand companies published this year: our intelligent platform understands your needs, learns your brand, and creates content that connects, while our smart assistant takes care of your customers around the clock. Every verb in that paragraph is borrowed, and a customer who has taken this course can translate it in seconds and trust it accordingly, which is to say, not much. Now the honest version, same facts, honest words: we use trained software to draft first versions of your content from examples of work that performed well. A person here grades every draft, checks every date and figure, and sends only what passes. The software predicts; we judge; you get the speed of the first and the responsibility of the second. Read those two paragraphs side by side and ask which company you would hand money to. The honest version is not weaker. It is stronger in the only way that survives contact with reality, because every claim in it can be checked, and the checking will go well. That is the commercial secret the fog merchants have backwards: in a market full of magic, the plain description is the differentiator. Your customers are being fogged by everyone. Be the one whose words still mean something at the end of the month. No magic in your copy is not a constraint on your marketing. It is, I have come to believe, the best marketing available to a small company in this field, because it is the only copy in the county that a careful reader cannot translate into nothing.

One more application, inward this time, because the vocabulary governs how you talk to yourself and your people, not only how you read strangers. When a tool errs in your business, the fog vocabulary offers you two useless sentences: the system is hopeless, which is menace turned inward, and the system is brilliant but moody, which is magic with an excuse attached. The honest vocabulary offers a better one: the prediction failed on a case outside its examples, or inside them at the rate the scoreboard already knew, and here is what we change, the pile, the check, the examples we feed the next version. That sentence leads somewhere. It has handles. Teams that speak it get better at using the machinery month by month, and teams that speak fog stay exactly as good as the day they bought it, because fog sentences have no handles and nothing to revise. Language is the steering wheel of a small company more than of a large one, because in a small company the owner's words become everyone's instructions by Friday. Set the vocabulary at the top and the clarity compounds downward. That, more than any single purchase, is the return on this course, and it starts the first time you catch a fog word in your own mouth and translate it before it lands. I still catch them in mine. The discipline is not a destination. It is a practice, like grading, like checking the five things, like every other professional habit this course has tried to install.

Let me give the two fog words their final examination, separately, because each deserves its own closing argument. Magic, examined, is always a claim about the speaker, never about the system. It says: I will not show you the workings, either because I cannot, which is ignorance, or because I will not, which is salesmanship. Neither deserves your money at the price wonder commands. And notice what the honest vocabulary does to wonder itself: it does not kill it, it relocates it. The real wonder in this field is not that a machine seems to think. It is that adjusted numbers, set by showing a function enough examples, can draft in your voice, rank your morning, and find the parking complaint hiding in four hundred reviews. That is wonderful the way flight is wonderful: more wonderful with the engineering visible, not less. Menace, examined, is the mirror claim. It says: I will show you intentions instead of workings, because intentions frighten and workings inform, and frightened audiences stay for the next instalment while informed ones go back to work. The honest reply to menace is not reassurance; reassurance is just magic with a kind face. The honest reply is the map from lesson five: here is where it is strong, here is where it is brittle, here is the boundary, and here is the human standing on it. A risk with an address can be managed. A menace can only be dreaded, and dread, like wonder, is a product somebody is selling. Refuse both products. Buy machinery, grade it, watch its edges, and let the theatre play to emptier rooms. That is the whole politics of this course, and it fits in one breath because the vocabulary carries it.

And a last word about the word intelligence itself, to close the circle we opened in lesson one. We are not going to win the renaming of a seventy-year-old field, and I am not asking you to try. The phrase artificial intelligence is in the name of this very course, and it will stay in the language long after both of us. The discipline was never to ban the phrase. It is to hear it, every time, with the translation running underneath, the way a person who knows a second language hears their first one still. Artificial intelligence, and underneath: programs that learn patterns from examples. A model, and underneath: a function with a memory of examples. It knows, and underneath: it predicts, from patterns, and here is its scoreboard. Two layers, always, the public word and the honest machinery, and you are never again at the mercy of the top layer alone. That bilingual hearing is the actual diploma of AI Fundamentals. Everything else, the definitions, the piles, the drills, was scaffolding to build it. You can take the scaffolding down now. The hearing stays.

One farewell exercise, the smallest in the course and the one I predict you will use most: the one-breath summary. Whenever you must explain to a partner, a customer, or yourself what one of these systems is doing in your business, say it in one breath, in honest words, in this shape: it is a model, trained on examples of this, that predicts that, and we grade it by counting this. Watch it work. It is a model, trained on examples of our past enquiries, that predicts which new enquiries deserve the first call, and we grade it by counting how many of its top calls became clients. One breath, no fog, and every important fact present: the thing, its examples, its act, its scoreboard. If a claim about any system cannot be said in that shape, the claim is not ready to be believed, including, especially, your own claims at the end of a hopeful day. Practise the breath until it is rude to do otherwise in your own head. Then teach it to one other person, because clarity compounds fastest when it is given away, and a course like this one is only ever a way of lending a vocabulary from one mind to another until the second mind no longer needs the loan.

And since a last lesson should leave the door open rather than close it, here is what your vocabulary unlocks next, stated plainly so you can hear your own progress. The next classes in this department will speak of how machines learn from data in greater depth, and you will not need their first hour, because you own their first principles. They will speak of data and where it lives and what it proves, and you will already be asking whose examples, labelled by whom, checked how. They will speak of agents, systems that act in the world through tools, and you will see the predictor inside the actor from the first minute, and ask the only question that matters about it: what does it predict, what can it touch when it is wrong, and who is standing on the boundary. That is the sound of a fundamentals course paying interest. Foundations are invisible when they work. You will simply find, class after class, that the new material lands faster for you than for the person who skipped the fog-clearing, because none of your attention is being spent on costumes. Spend it all on the machinery. There is plenty of machinery, it is genuinely interesting, and some of it, I will confess at the door of my own course, is beautiful, in the plain, unmagical way that well-made things are beautiful when you finally see how they work.

Keep the vocabulary the way you keep a good tool: oiled, in reach, and lent out carefully. It will dull if you stop using it, because the fog is patient and it publishes every day. But it sharpens just as reliably, one translation at a time, and every headline you translate without thinking is proof the sharpening is holding. That is all any teacher can honestly promise at the end of a course: not that you will never be fogged again, but that you now own the means of clearing it yourself, in your own head, at the speed of reading.

Recap, in order, and this recap carries the whole course with it, so take it slowly. Lesson one: artificial intelligence names programs that learn patterns from examples, machinery, mathematics running at enormous scale on data, and prediction is not understanding. Lesson two: three ingredients, data the examples, parameters the settings, training the showing, and garbage in means garbage out. Lesson three: a model is a function with a memory of examples, embodied rather than stored, able to generalise and unable to show its evidence. Lesson four: prediction is the core act, training in the workshop and prediction in the wild, and predictions can be graded while understandings cannot. Lesson five: strong where cases resemble the examples, brittle where they depart, one design with two faces, and you are the boundary detector. Lesson six, today: the honest vocabulary holds all of it, knows becomes predicts, understands becomes was shaped by, and no magic and no menace are permitted to stand where machinery can be named.

What comes next is the questions on this lesson, the last set of the course, and the full text stays open beside them, as it has every time; going back to read is learning, not cheating, and never more than today, because today's questions reach back across everything we built. When you finish them, you will have finished AI Fundamentals, and the department's next classes will be waiting, and they will speak to you in the words you now own. I have enjoyed this room. Come back and visit it whenever a headline tries to fog you; the vocabulary will be here, and so will the sentence we started with, the whole secret in one line: a model is a function that was shown so many examples that its guesses became good, and training is the showing. You know it now the way you know your own trade: from the inside. Class dismissed, and well done. Go and use the words well, grade what you use, watch the boundaries, and when the fog rolls in, as it will, remember that you know how it is made now, and anything whose making you know has already lost most of its power over you.
